screens.title: Deep Dive into Amazon CloudFront
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn how Amazon CloudFront speeds up and secures web and media delivery worldwide. CloudFront places cached copies of your objects at edge locations, so users receive faster responses and your origin servers handle less load. We will cover distribution types, common origin choices such as S3 and custom HTTP servers, and the configuration knobs—cache behaviors, TTLs, and cache keys—that control freshness and correctness. Security is equally central: you will see how to enforce HTTPS for viewers, request TLS to origins, and use Origin Access Control to lock down S3 buckets so only CloudFront can read them. Practical decisions matter: choosing what headers, cookies, and query strings to forward affects both correctness and cache hit ratio. Finally, you will follow a step-by-step lab that deploys a static site to S3 and creates a CloudFront web distribution with OAC so you can test secure, accelerated delivery. By the end, you should be able to explain CloudFront’s role, choose appropriate settings for dynamic versus static content, and apply basic security controls that protect origin data. What content in your environment would benefit first from a CDN?

screens.title: What is Amazon CloudFront?
screens.narratorSegment: CloudFront is a global Content Delivery Network that caches and delivers web assets from edge locations close to users. At its core, CloudFront stores copies of objects at edge locations and serves requests from the nearest edge when possible, which reduces latency and the number of requests that reach your origin. For a concrete example, imagine an image hosted in an S3 bucket in one AWS region. When users in another continent request that image, CloudFront routes them to the nearest edge location. If the image is cached there, it's returned instantly; if not, CloudFront fetches it from the origin, caches it at the edge, and returns it. A common misconception is to assume CloudFront always reduces origin cost linearly; in practice, poorly chosen TTLs or forwarding rules can increase origin requests. The takeaway is simple: CloudFront provides proximity-based delivery and caching, but your configuration—cache TTLs, cache keys, and what you forward—determines correctness and cost. As you plan a distribution, ask whether the content is static or dynamic, how often it changes, and who needs personalized responses. What is Amazon CloudFront? means cloudfront caches content at edge locations to deliver it faster and reduce origin load; configuration controls freshness and correctness.. In practical terms, definition, role, and a concrete delivery example. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.2 › What is Amazon CloudFront?
Definition

CloudFront is a CDN that caches content at edge locations worldwide. It routes viewer requests to the nearest edge location, serving cached objects when available and retrieving them from the origin when not.

How it works
  • Viewer requests content.
  • CloudFront routes to nearest Edge Location.
  • If cached, serve directly; otherwise fetch from origin and cache.
Concrete example
An image in an S3 bucket is requested by users worldwide. CloudFront caches a copy at an edge region and serves it to subsequent viewers without contacting the S3 origin each time.
Key Takeaway

CloudFront reduces latency by delivering cached content from edge locations; your cache choices determine freshness and origin load.

Common misconception

Assuming any cache means no origin load. In practice, cache misses and inappropriate TTLs can still generate significant origin traffic. Configure TTLs and cache keys to avoid unexpected origin requests.

Try this

Identify one static asset and one dynamic API in your app. Predict how often each should refresh in cache and why.

Example response flow
GET /images/logo.png  → Edge Location
If cached: 200 OK from CloudFront cache
If not cached: CloudFront GET origin (S3) → cache → 200 OK to viewer

screens.title: Distribution types and origins
screens.narratorSegment: When you create a CloudFront distribution you must choose an origin. The most common pattern for modern web apps is a Web Distribution tied to either an S3 bucket for static assets or a custom HTTP/HTTPS origin for dynamic content. Use an S3 origin for assets like images, styles, and static H T M L because S3 offers simple object storage and CloudFront can fetch and cache objects directly. For dynamic APIs or server-side rendered pages, use a custom HTTP origin—often an ALB fronting EC2 or containers—because the origin can process application logic and return tailored responses. A common mistake is selecting S3 for content that requires per-user personalization; S3 cannot generate dynamic responses, and relying on query strings or cookies alone may complicate the cache key. Another nuance: for S3 origins you can and should enable Origin Access Control to prevent direct public reads, while custom origins should be configured to accept HTTPS and validate CloudFront-specific headers when possible. The practical question is: does the origin need to compute per-request state? If yes, use a custom origin and design cache behaviors carefully.

keyIdea.title: Origin guidance
keyIdea.text: Select S3 for static objects and custom HTTP/HTTPS origins for dynamic or compute-driven responses; align the origin choice with content volatility and personalization needs.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.2 › Distribution types and origins
S3 Origin (Static)
Best for static website hosting, images, and media files. CloudFront can fetch objects directly from S3 and cache them at edge locations, reducing latency and origin bandwidth.
When to use
Static assets, content that doesn't require per-request computation, and sites where long TTLs are acceptable.
Security note
Enable OAC to restrict direct S3 access; do not leave the bucket publicly readable when OAC is available.
Custom HTTP/HTTPS Origin (Dynamic)
Use when your origin must run code to produce responses, such as APIs, server-side rendered pages, or media packaging endpoints. Configure HTTPS to origin and consider custom headers for validation.
When to use
APIs, personalized content, or when you need origin-side logic; set short TTLs and forward specific cookies/headers.
Security note
Use HTTPS to origin and optional custom headers to confirm requests come from your CloudFront distribution.
Common mistake

Using an S3 origin for content that requires per-user personalization leads to either incorrect cached responses or requiring heavy forwarding that destroys the cache hit ratio.

Key Takeaway

Match origin type to content needs: static and cache-friendly go to S3; dynamic and personalized go to custom HTTP origins with careful cache policy design.

screens.title: Cache behaviors and path patterns
screens.narratorSegment: Cache behaviors are the routing and processing rules that tell CloudFront how to handle requests matching specific URL path patterns. Each distribution has a single default cache behavior and you can add additional behaviors for targeted path patterns like /images/* or /api/*. For each behavior you select an origin, a viewer protocol policy, allowed HTTP methods, and a cache policy. The path pattern determines which requests follow the behavior’s rules; the default behavior handles anything else. A concrete example: you might create a behavior for /api/* that points to an ALB origin, allows POST and other methods, and uses a custom cache policy with a short TTL and selected session cookies forwarded. For static assets, a behavior for /static/* could use an S3 origin, GET/HEAD only, and long TTLs. Misconceptions arise when teams over-index on many tiny behaviors—too many behaviors can complicate testing and maintenance. The practical approach is to keep behaviors coarse and use cache policies to handle differences in caching. Cache behaviors and path patterns means use cache behaviors to map url patterns to origins and caching rules; prefer coarse, maintainable patterns and adjust cache policies for finer control.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 11 › Chapter 11.2 › Cache behaviors and path patterns
Behavior process
1
Define path patterns
Create rules like /images/*, /api/*, or *.html to group requests that should be handled similarly.
2
Assign origins
For each pattern pick the origin CloudFront will contact when the object is not cached.
3
Configure viewer protocol and methods
Enforce HTTPS and choose allowed HTTP methods; APIs often need POST and OPTIONS while static assets need only GET and HEAD.
4
Attach cache policy
Select or create cache policies to control TTLs and which headers, cookies, and query strings are included in the cache key.
Example
Default behavior → origin A, /api/* → ALB origin with POST/PUT allowed and short TTL, /static/* → S3 origin with GET/HEAD only and long TTL.
Key Takeaway

Map coarse path patterns to origins and use cache policies for per-response caching rules to keep configuration manageable.

screens.title: Cache policy mechanics and TTLs
screens.narratorSegment: Cache policies control how CloudFront caches objects and what makes one cached object distinct from another. Three TTL values are central: minimum TTL prevents CloudFront from revalidating too quickly, default TTL is how long an object is cached when the origin doesn't supply caching headers, and maximum TTL caps how long CloudFront may keep an object regardless of origin hints. For example, static images might use a high default and maximum TTL, while A P I responses require a low default TTL to avoid serving stale data. A frequent error is setting all TTLs very high for content that changes frequently; the result is stale content in edge caches. Another mistake is setting TTLs too low for static assets, which increases origin load and defeats CDN benefits. When creating a cache policy, base TTLs on content volatility: infrequently changing files get long TTLs; dynamic or personalized content gets short TTLs or is excluded from caching. Try this: pick an asset and reason through an appropriate min/default/max TTL that balances freshness and origin cost. Cache policy mechanics and TTLs means use ttls to align cache duration with content volatility—long for stable static files, short for dynamic responses—to balance freshness and origin load.. In practical terms, minimum, default, and maximum ttl explained. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.2 › Cache policy mechanics and TTLs
TTL definitions
  • Minimum TTL: the shortest time CloudFront will keep an object before considering revalidation.
  • Default TTL: the caching time used when the origin provides no cache-control headers.
  • Maximum TTL: a ceiling on caching regardless of origin headers.
Example choices

Image assets: min 3600s, default 86400s, max 31536000s. API responses: min 0s, default 60s, max 300s. Adjust based on update cadence.

Common mistake

Setting TTLs uniformly high for everything causes stale dynamic content. Conversely, setting TTLs too low removes caching benefits and increases origin load.

Key Takeaway

Choose TTLs based on how often content changes. Use low TTLs for dynamic data and long TTLs for stable static assets.

screens.title: Cache keys: headers, query strings, and cookies
screens.narratorSegment: A cache key is the identifier CloudFront uses to decide whether a cached object matches a viewer request. By default the cache key may include URI and host, but you can add headers, query strings, and cookies. Forwarding more request elements increases correctness for personalized or variant responses but reduces cache hit ratio because each unique combination can create a distinct cache entry. For example, if your A P I response changes per Authorization header, you must forward that header and include it in the cache key; failing to do so leads to incorrect responses served to different users. Conversely, forwarding all headers and cookies as a blanket policy is a common mistake that fragments the cache and increases origin requests. The practical guidance is to forward only those headers, cookies, or query strings that your origin relies on to vary responses. When in doubt, start with none or a minimal set, test correctness, and then add specific fields when required. Cache keys: headers, query strings, and cookies means forward only the headers, cookies, and query strings required to produce correct responses; extra forwarding harms cache efficiency.. In practical terms, what to forward and why it matters for cache hits. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 11 › Chapter 11.2 › Cache keys: headers, query strings, and cookies
What makes a cache key
A cache key is built from request parts you include: the request path, and optionally selected headers, query strings, and cookies. Each unique key is a separate item in edge cache storage.
Concrete example
An API that varies by session cookie must have that session cookie forwarded and included in the cache key. Otherwise, CloudFront may return another user's cached response.
Best practice
Start with minimal forwarding. Add only the headers, query strings, or cookies necessary to preserve correctness, then monitor cache hit ratios.
Common mistake

Forwarding all headers or cookies to be safe often collapses the cache hit ratio because each request appears unique.

Pro tip

Use selective forwarding for personalization and keep static assets entirely separate with their own cache behavior.

screens.title: Hands-on: Deploy a static site with CloudFront and OAC
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on walkthrough describes creating a static site in S3, creating a CloudFront web distribution that uses Origin Access Control, and applying the suggested bucket policy. Start by creating a uniquely named S3 bucket and uploading a simple index. html and one image. Do not enable block-all-public-access at first so you can test and then apply OAC to restrict access. In CloudFront, create a web distribution and select the S3 bucket as the origin. Choose to use OAC and create a new OAC with defaults; CloudFront will provide a bucket policy you must copy. Set the viewer protocol policy to redirect HTTP to HTTPS and enter index. html as the default root object. While the distribution deploys, paste the provided policy into the S3 bucket policy editor to grant CloudFront read permissions and prevent direct public reads. After deployment, visiting the distribution domain should show your site while direct S3 URLs are denied. A common mistake is not applying the bucket policy correctly—verify the distribution ID in the policy before saving. This lab reinforces how CloudFront and OAC improve performance and security.

screens.title: Security: HTTPS, ACM, and Origin TLS
screens.narratorSegment: Securing data in transit is essential. CloudFront lets you enforce HTTPS to viewers and use free SSL/TLS certificates from AWS Certificate Manager for custom domains. Set the viewer protocol policy to redirect HTTP to HTTPS or require HTTPS only to ensure confidentiality and integrity between users and the CDN. For connections between CloudFront and your origin, configure CloudFront to use HTTPS to the origin when possible so origin traffic is encrypted as well. For S3 origins, Origin Access Control is the recommended approach to prevent direct public S3 reads—CloudFront signs requests to S3 so only CloudFront can retrieve objects. A common misconception is assuming HTTPS to viewers protects everything; you must also secure origin connections and lock S3 bucket policies with OAC to prevent direct origin exposure. The practical step is to request an ACM certificate in the region CloudFront requires, attach it to the distribution, and enable OAC for S3 origins. This combination protects data on both legs of delivery and prevents accidental public access. Module 11 › Chapter 11.2 › Security: HTTPS, ACM, and Origin TLS
Viewer security

Use ACM certificates for your custom domain and set CloudFront viewer protocol policy to Redirect HTTP to HTTPS or HTTPS Only to guarantee encrypted viewer connections.

Why it matters
HTTPS protects user data in transit and is required for many browser features and security expectations from users and compliance regimes.
Origin security

Configure CloudFront to use HTTPS for origin connections when possible, and for S3 use Origin Access Control so the bucket allows reads only from your distribution.

Common mistake
Assuming HTTPS to viewers is enough. If the origin is publicly readable or origin connections are unencrypted, content or credentials may be exposed.
Key Takeaway

Use ACM for viewer TLS, enforce HTTPS, and use OAC or TLS to origin to protect both viewer and origin legs of delivery.

screens.title: Compression and performance optimizations
screens.narratorSegment: Reducing payload size improves perceived and actual performance. CloudFront supports compression such as Gzip and Brotli to send smaller payloads to viewers when their clients support it. Enable compression so text-based assets like H T M L, C S S, and JavaScript are delivered more quickly and consume less bandwidth. Another practical optimization is to split static and dynamic assets into separate behaviors: aggressive caching and long TTLs for compressed static files, conservative TTLs for dynamic endpoints. A common misconception is that compression alone solves slow load times; compression helps but does not replace good caching policies, origin performance, or network optimization. Also note that pre-compressing and storing compressed versions in the origin can be useful when your origin or build system already outputs compressed assets. The key question is which assets will benefit from compression and whether pre-compressing or runtime compression offers the best trade-off for your workflow. Module 11 › Chapter 11.2 › Compression and performance optimizations
Compression choices
Enable Gzip or Brotli in CloudFront so compatible browsers receive compressed responses. Text assets benefit most: HTML, CSS, JS, JSON, and SVG.
Pre-compress vs runtime
If your build pipeline produces compressed files, serve pre-compressed assets from the origin. Otherwise enable CloudFront compression at delivery time.
Combine with caching
Compressed static assets should have long TTLs and be served from S3 origin with aggressive caching. Dynamic endpoints should avoid long TTLs even if compressed.
Key Takeaway

Compression reduces payloads; pair it with sensible cache policies so compression benefits are consistent and cost-effective.

screens.title: Common mistakes and safety notes
screens.narratorSegment: CloudFront helps performance and security, but common misconfigurations undercut those benefits. First, incorrect caching: long TTLs for dynamic content cause stale pages, while very short TTLs on static content cause unnecessary origin load. Second, origin access misconfiguration: leaving an S3 bucket public instead of using OAC permits direct reads and undermines access controls. Third, forwarding all headers, query strings, or cookies without need fragments the cache and lowers hit ratios, leading to higher latency and origin cost. Fourth, not enforcing HTTPS leaves viewer connections unprotected; use ACM and viewer protocol policy to redirect or require HTTPS. Finally, performance bottlenecks can still occur during cache misses if the origin is slow—CloudFront offloads many requests but cannot fix a slow origin. The practical remedy is to audit cache behaviors and policies, apply OAC for S3, selectively forward request elements, and monitor cache-hit ratios and origin request rates. Ask yourself: which misconfiguration would most impact our users right now and how quickly can we fix it? Common mistakes and safety notes means avoid stale or insecure deployments by aligning ttls with content volatility, using oac for s3, selectively forwarding request elements, and enforcing https.. In practical terms, configuration pitfalls that cause stale content, security gaps, or poor caching. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Module 11 › Chapter 11.2 › Common mistakes and safety notes
Frequent pitfalls
  • Overly long TTLs for dynamic content causing stale data.
  • Leaving S3 publicly readable instead of implementing OAC.
  • Forwarding everything (headers/cookies/query strings) and destroying cache efficiency.
  • Not enforcing HTTPS for viewers or origin connections.
Monitoring and remediation
Watch cache hit ratios, origin request rates, and latency. When issues appear, verify TTLs, cache key composition, OAC status, and whether the origin itself is slow.
Action

Run an audit: confirm OAC is applied, check TTLs per behavior, and review what you forward in the cache key.

screens.title: Assessment scenario and reasoning
screens.narratorSegment: This assessment-style scenario asks you to reason about cache behavior choices. Imagine a web application behind an ALB serving personalized pages based on a session cookie, and static assets in S3. The correct approach splits traffic: create a behavior for /api/* and personalized pages that forwards specific session cookies and selects a short TTL, and create a separate /static/* behavior that points to S3 with long TTLs and no cookies forwarded. Why this works: forwarding the session cookie for personalized pages ensures correct responses per user, and isolating static assets into their own behavior preserves cache efficiency. A wrong answer is to forward all headers and cookies globally; that big forwarding scope fragments edge caches and increases origin requests. When answering configuration questions, explain which parts of the request must be considered in the cache key, how TTLs match volatility, and how origins map to behavior patterns. This reasoning demonstrates both correctness and an understanding of cache performance trade-offs. Scenario

Personalized web app served behind an ALB, static assets on S3. Session cookie determines per-user content; static assets are identical across users.

Recommended config

Separating behaviors keeps personalization correct while preserving cache efficiency for shared static content.

screens.narratorSegment: Keep three ideas front of mind as you design CloudFront distributions. First, CloudFront is a global CDN that serves cached content from edge locations to reduce latency and origin load. Second, cache behavior and cache policy choices—path patterns, TTLs, and which headers, query strings, and cookies you forward—determine both correctness and cache efficiency. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn how Amazon CloudFront speeds up and secures web and media delivery worldwide. CloudFront places cached copies of your objects at edge locations, so users receive faster responses and your origin servers handle less load. We will cover distribution types, common origin choices such as S3 and custom HTTP servers, and the configuration knobs—cache behaviors, TTLs, and cache keys—that control freshness and correctness. Security is equally central: you will see how to enforce HTTPS for viewers, request TLS to origins, and use Origin Access Control to lock down S3 buckets so only CloudFront can read them. Practical decisions matter: choosing what headers, cookies, and query strings to forward affects both correctness and cache hit ratio. Finally, you will follow a step-by-step lab that deploys a static site to S3 and creates a CloudFront web distribution with OAC so you can test secure, accelerated delivery. By the end, you should be able to explain CloudFront’s role, choose appropriate settings for dynamic versus static content, and apply basic security controls that protect origin data. What content in your environment would benefit first from a CDN?

These objectives map to practical skills you will use when designing and operating CloudFront distributions. First, you will be able to explain CloudFront’s core functionality: how edge caching reduces latency and origin load. Second, you will learn to choose distribution types and origins, and to justify when to use an S3 origin versus a custom HTTP origin behind an ALB. Third, you will practice configuring cache behaviors and policies—setting path patterns, TTLs, and deciding what to forward in the cache key. Finally on this screen you will begin to apply basic security controls like enforcing HTTPS and preparing for Origin Access Control. Each objective is a discrete competency you can verify after hands-on practice, and each sets up the next step: from explanation to configuration to secure deployment. As you work through the lab, check these competencies by observing reduced latency, correct personalized responses, and a locked-down bucket that denies direct public access.

This second objectives slide focuses on practical application: designing cache behaviors, choosing forwarding rules, and performing a secure deployment using Origin Access Control. You will learn to map URL path patterns to specific origins and behaviors so that static files can be aggressively cached while APIs remain dynamic with short TTLs. You will also practice creating custom cache policies when managed policies are insufficient, learning how minimum, maximum, and default TTL values interact to control freshness and origin traffic. Finally, this screen highlights testing and verification: deploying a static S3 site, creating a CloudFront web distribution with OAC, applying the provided bucket policy, and confirming direct S3 access is denied. These applied skills turn architecture decisions into repeatable operational steps. Learning Objectives — Applied Skills means design cache behavior rules and policies that balance freshness and cache efficiency, and verify secure origin access using oac.. In practical terms, from configuration choices to secure deployments. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

CloudFront is a global Content Delivery Network that caches and delivers web assets from edge locations close to users. At its core, CloudFront stores copies of objects at edge locations and serves requests from the nearest edge when possible, which reduces latency and the number of requests that reach your origin. For a concrete example, imagine an image hosted in an S3 bucket in one AWS region. When users in another continent request that image, CloudFront routes them to the nearest edge location. If the image is cached there, it's returned instantly; if not, CloudFront fetches it from the origin, caches it at the edge, and returns it. A common misconception is to assume CloudFront always reduces origin cost linearly; in practice, poorly chosen TTLs or forwarding rules can increase origin requests. The takeaway is simple: CloudFront provides proximity-based delivery and caching, but your configuration—cache TTLs, cache keys, and what you forward—determines correctness and cost. As you plan a distribution, ask whether the content is static or dynamic, how often it changes, and who needs personalized responses. What is Amazon CloudFront? means cloudfront caches content at edge locations to deliver it faster and reduce origin load; configuration controls freshness and correctness.. In practical terms, definition, role, and a concrete delivery example. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

When you create a CloudFront distribution you must choose an origin. The most common pattern for modern web apps is a Web Distribution tied to either an S3 bucket for static assets or a custom HTTP/HTTPS origin for dynamic content. Use an S3 origin for assets like images, styles, and static H T M L because S3 offers simple object storage and CloudFront can fetch and cache objects directly. For dynamic APIs or server-side rendered pages, use a custom HTTP origin—often an ALB fronting EC2 or containers—because the origin can process application logic and return tailored responses. A common mistake is selecting S3 for content that requires per-user personalization; S3 cannot generate dynamic responses, and relying on query strings or cookies alone may complicate the cache key. Another nuance: for S3 origins you can and should enable Origin Access Control to prevent direct public reads, while custom origins should be configured to accept HTTPS and validate CloudFront-specific headers when possible. The practical question is: does the origin need to compute per-request state? If yes, use a custom origin and design cache behaviors carefully.

Cache behaviors are the routing and processing rules that tell CloudFront how to handle requests matching specific URL path patterns. Each distribution has a single default cache behavior and you can add additional behaviors for targeted path patterns like /images/* or /api/*. For each behavior you select an origin, a viewer protocol policy, allowed HTTP methods, and a cache policy. The path pattern determines which requests follow the behavior’s rules; the default behavior handles anything else. A concrete example: you might create a behavior for /api/* that points to an ALB origin, allows POST and other methods, and uses a custom cache policy with a short TTL and selected session cookies forwarded. For static assets, a behavior for /static/* could use an S3 origin, GET/HEAD only, and long TTLs. Misconceptions arise when teams over-index on many tiny behaviors—too many behaviors can complicate testing and maintenance. The practical approach is to keep behaviors coarse and use cache policies to handle differences in caching. Cache behaviors and path patterns means use cache behaviors to map url patterns to origins and caching rules; prefer coarse, maintainable patterns and adjust cache policies for finer control.. In practical terms, how behaviors route requests and select origins. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Cache policies control how CloudFront caches objects and what makes one cached object distinct from another. Three TTL values are central: minimum TTL prevents CloudFront from revalidating too quickly, default TTL is how long an object is cached when the origin doesn't supply caching headers, and maximum TTL caps how long CloudFront may keep an object regardless of origin hints. For example, static images might use a high default and maximum TTL, while A P I responses require a low default TTL to avoid serving stale data. A frequent error is setting all TTLs very high for content that changes frequently; the result is stale content in edge caches. Another mistake is setting TTLs too low for static assets, which increases origin load and defeats CDN benefits. When creating a cache policy, base TTLs on content volatility: infrequently changing files get long TTLs; dynamic or personalized content gets short TTLs or is excluded from caching. Try this: pick an asset and reason through an appropriate min/default/max TTL that balances freshness and origin cost. Cache policy mechanics and TTLs means use ttls to align cache duration with content volatility—long for stable static files, short for dynamic responses—to balance freshness and origin load.. In practical terms, minimum, default, and maximum ttl explained. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A cache key is the identifier CloudFront uses to decide whether a cached object matches a viewer request. By default the cache key may include URI and host, but you can add headers, query strings, and cookies. Forwarding more request elements increases correctness for personalized or variant responses but reduces cache hit ratio because each unique combination can create a distinct cache entry. For example, if your A P I response changes per Authorization header, you must forward that header and include it in the cache key; failing to do so leads to incorrect responses served to different users. Conversely, forwarding all headers and cookies as a blanket policy is a common mistake that fragments the cache and increases origin requests. The practical guidance is to forward only those headers, cookies, or query strings that your origin relies on to vary responses. When in doubt, start with none or a minimal set, test correctness, and then add specific fields when required. Cache keys: headers, query strings, and cookies means forward only the headers, cookies, and query strings required to produce correct responses; extra forwarding harms cache efficiency.. In practical terms, what to forward and why it matters for cache hits. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

This hands-on walkthrough describes creating a static site in S3, creating a CloudFront web distribution that uses Origin Access Control, and applying the suggested bucket policy. Start by creating a uniquely named S3 bucket and uploading a simple index. html and one image. Do not enable block-all-public-access at first so you can test and then apply OAC to restrict access. In CloudFront, create a web distribution and select the S3 bucket as the origin. Choose to use OAC and create a new OAC with defaults; CloudFront will provide a bucket policy you must copy. Set the viewer protocol policy to redirect HTTP to HTTPS and enter index. html as the default root object. While the distribution deploys, paste the provided policy into the S3 bucket policy editor to grant CloudFront read permissions and prevent direct public reads. After deployment, visiting the distribution domain should show your site while direct S3 URLs are denied. A common mistake is not applying the bucket policy correctly—verify the distribution ID in the policy before saving. This lab reinforces how CloudFront and OAC improve performance and security.

Securing data in transit is essential. CloudFront lets you enforce HTTPS to viewers and use free SSL/TLS certificates from AWS Certificate Manager for custom domains. Set the viewer protocol policy to redirect HTTP to HTTPS or require HTTPS only to ensure confidentiality and integrity between users and the CDN. For connections between CloudFront and your origin, configure CloudFront to use HTTPS to the origin when possible so origin traffic is encrypted as well. For S3 origins, Origin Access Control is the recommended approach to prevent direct public S3 reads—CloudFront signs requests to S3 so only CloudFront can retrieve objects. A common misconception is assuming HTTPS to viewers protects everything; you must also secure origin connections and lock S3 bucket policies with OAC to prevent direct origin exposure. The practical step is to request an ACM certificate in the region CloudFront requires, attach it to the distribution, and enable OAC for S3 origins. This combination protects data on both legs of delivery and prevents accidental public access. Reducing payload size improves perceived and actual performance. CloudFront supports compression such as Gzip and Brotli to send smaller payloads to viewers when their clients support it. Enable compression so text-based assets like H T M L, C S S, and JavaScript are delivered more quickly and consume less bandwidth. Another practical optimization is to split static and dynamic assets into separate behaviors: aggressive caching and long TTLs for compressed static files, conservative TTLs for dynamic endpoints. A common misconception is that compression alone solves slow load times; compression helps but does not replace good caching policies, origin performance, or network optimization. Also note that pre-compressing and storing compressed versions in the origin can be useful when your origin or build system already outputs compressed assets. The key question is which assets will benefit from compression and whether pre-compressing or runtime compression offers the best trade-off for your workflow. CloudFront helps performance and security, but common misconfigurations undercut those benefits. First, incorrect caching: long TTLs for dynamic content cause stale pages, while very short TTLs on static content cause unnecessary origin load. Second, origin access misconfiguration: leaving an S3 bucket public instead of using OAC permits direct reads and undermines access controls. Third, forwarding all headers, query strings, or cookies without need fragments the cache and lowers hit ratios, leading to higher latency and origin cost. Fourth, not enforcing HTTPS leaves viewer connections unprotected; use ACM and viewer protocol policy to redirect or require HTTPS. Finally, performance bottlenecks can still occur during cache misses if the origin is slow—CloudFront offloads many requests but cannot fix a slow origin. The practical remedy is to audit cache behaviors and policies, apply OAC for S3, selectively forward request elements, and monitor cache-hit ratios and origin request rates. Ask yourself: which misconfiguration would most impact our users right now and how quickly can we fix it? This assessment-style scenario asks you to reason about cache behavior choices. Imagine a web application behind an ALB serving personalized pages based on a session cookie, and static assets in S3. The correct approach splits traffic: create a behavior for /api/* and personalized pages that forwards specific session cookies and selects a short TTL, and create a separate /static/* behavior that points to S3 with long TTLs and no cookies forwarded. Why this works: forwarding the session cookie for personalized pages ensures correct responses per user, and isolating static assets into their own behavior preserves cache efficiency. A wrong answer is to forward all headers and cookies globally; that big forwarding scope fragments edge caches and increases origin requests. When answering configuration questions, explain which parts of the request must be considered in the cache key, how TTLs match volatility, and how origins map to behavior patterns. Keep three ideas front of mind as you design CloudFront distributions. First, CloudFront is a global CDN that serves cached content from edge locations to reduce latency and origin load. Second, cache behavior and cache policy choices—path patterns, TTLs, and which headers, query strings, and cookies you forward—determine both correctness and cache efficiency. Third, secure your origins: enforce HTTPS for viewer connections, use TLS to origin where possible, and apply Origin Access Control for S3 so CloudFront alone can read your objects. Together these concepts balance performance, correctness, and security. Whenever you configure a distribution, ask: which origin should I use, which requests must vary responses, and how will TTLs affect freshness and origin load? Answering those three questions will guide practical, safe CloudFront deployments. Before you finish, commit three compact reminders to memory. First, design your cache key consciously: forward only the headers, query strings, and cookies required for correctness. Second, match TTLs to content volatility: long for static, short for dynamic, and avoid extremes that cause stale data or unnecessary origin load. Third, secure origins: enforce HTTPS and use Origin Access Control for S3 so CloudFront is the only path to your objects. These three checks—cache key, TTL alignment, and origin security—cover the most common operational mistakes and ensure CloudFront improves both performance and security for global users.
